public_rationale: Relevant principled arguments existed before the post. One addressed indefinite stability when synthetic data accumulate; another explained how intermediate generation expands reasoning power. Neither cleanly establishes the claim's contextual target of continued pretraining scaling overcoming the listed limitations. Conversely, finding limitations or failing to locate a matching argument cannot establish that none ever existed. Broader readings of scaling or synthetic-data sufficiency would make these papers stronger counterexamples.
limitations: The claim concerns the existence of arguments, not whether those arguments ultimately proved correct.
The literature search is not exhaustive.
The outcome depends materially on the scope of scaling and indefinite sufficiency.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: There has never been a principled argument that scaling would solve hallucinations, reasoning, or open-world edge cases, or that synthetic data would suffice indefinitely.

statement.excerpt: Crucially, there has never been any principled argument that they would solve hallucinations or reasoning, or edge cases in open-ended worlds —or that synthetic data would suffice indefinitely to keep feeding the machine.
statement.document_title: An AI rumor you won’t want to miss

from_speaker: there has never been any principled argument
they would solve hallucinations or reasoning
our_interpretation: This is a claim about arguments available through 2024-11-10, not about whether later models actually solved these problems.
A principled argument means a reasoned theoretical or empirical case with stated assumptions. It need not be a proof or an accepted conclusion.

In context, scaling means increasing pretraining data, model resources and training compute. Results requiring a different inference procedure are relevant qualifications but do not automatically settle this claim.
Solve means overcome the named limitation, rather than merely improve a benchmark score.

I read indefinitely feeding the machine in the surrounding scaling discussion as sustaining useful continued scaling. Avoiding degradation alone may satisfy a broader reading, so that ambiguity is material.
criteria.support_condition: A sufficiently comprehensive assessment of the pre-post literature establishes that no principled argument addressed any of the listed outcomes at the claimed scope.
criteria.contradiction_condition: At least one argument published by 2024-11-10 gives a principled case that the relevant scaling process would overcome a listed limitation or that synthetic data could sustain useful scaling indefinitely. A guarantee is not required.

evidence.explanation: The paper bounds error independently of the number of retraining iterations in a linear-model setting that retains previous data. This is a principled argument for indefinite stability under assumptions, but it does not establish indefinite capability gains from synthetic data.

evidence.locator: Abstract, answer to whether intermediate generation extends computational power
evidence.explanation: The paper gives a theoretical account of how additional intermediate tokens expand transformers' computational power. This challenges a broad claim that no principled reasoning argument existed, but does not show that increasing pretraining resources alone supplies the needed learned procedure.

The paper identifies conditional statistical limits for hallucinations of arbitrary facts while distinguishing systematic and repeated facts. It neither proves that all hallucinations survive scaling nor establishes that no contrary principled argument existed.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: A pre-2024-11-10 argument explicitly connecting the claimed scaling process to one listed outcome would contradict the categorical claim. Supporting it would require a substantially more comprehensive historical review with clear definitions.
